title: The Art of Telling a Good Story
author: Antonius Veritas
summary: In this entry on social skills, Antonius Veritas argues that storytelling is a learnable skill that makes ideas memorable and helps people understand one another. He uses Aesop's fable of the crow and the pitcher to show how a few sentences can carry desperation, hope, disappointment and a solution. His advice has four parts: lead with drama and stakes, give a character's thoughts, emotions and actions in detail, tell the story with energy and a willingness to look foolish, and sometimes let a story carry a lesson. He draws on Dostoyevsky's White Nights and Robert Greene's practice of appending stories to his arguments. The closing warning is that people sabotage themselves by assuming they are either natural storytellers or not, and so never practise.
points: A story holds attention when it begins with stakes and then moves through obstacles and failed attempts, so the listener hopes and despairs along with the character.
Structure is the main failure point: rambling delivery forces listeners to work out which details matter.
Revealing a character's thoughts, fears and mistakes lets listeners empathise, but irrelevant detail makes a story tiring.
Energy, pauses and imitation make the listener feel present, which requires the speaker to risk looking foolish.
Stories carry moral lessons more gently than lectures, and the skill improves with practice rather than talent alone.
quotes: What pulls me into a story is when someone starts with something dramatic. I’m not a big fan of slow build-ups. Stakes, surprises, and uncertainty give me the most visceral effect.
People often fall into the trap of lacking structure. They say whatever comes into their minds in a haphazard way, which leaves everyone confused, wondering what the story is even about.
A good storyteller makes that work easier. We know what someone wants, what’s getting in their way, and why they’ve decided to do something about it.
It’s good to reveal enough for someone to relate or feel something. Our embarrassment, fear, mistakes, and less admirable motives can explain the decisions that follow.

This requires a willingness to look foolish. Sometimes the best part is the confidence with which you made a terrible decision, or the elaborate explanation you offered when everyone already knew you were lying.
We can pass on moral lessons to our children, give cautionary tales to family members, and help friends consider a decision without making the conversation feel like a lecture.
Yet people sabotage themselves by deciding either they’re naturals at story-telling or not. They don’t like practicing, so they rarely give themselves a chance to improve.
